title: Mouse Tubuloid Model for Myoglobinuric Acute Kidney Injury
author: Torres Pereiro, Zhou, et al.
materials: Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium High glucose

steps.title: Prepare Myoglobin Solution
steps.instruction: Reduce equine skeletal muscle myoglobin to deoxy‑myoglobin and make a 20 mg ml⁻¹ working solution containing 0.75 mM Vitamin C.

substeps.instruction: Weigh the required amount of myoglobin powder in a sterile 50 ml tube (use a 15 ml tube if <100 mg).
Add tubuloid culture medium, flushing the tube walls to ensure no powder remains, and incubate at room temperature (RT) on a tube roller for 30 min; solution should turn brownish.
Sonicate the suspension with three 5‑second pulses, allowing 10–15 s breaks between pulses; keep the sonicator tip inside the liquid to avoid excess bubbles.
If visible particles persist, incubate an additional 30 min at RT on the roller.

Add L‑ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) to reach a final concentration of 0.75 mM (stock: 300 mM Vitamin C in Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺‑free PBS, prepared in warm PBS, incubated 1–2 h on a roller, aliquoted and stored at –20 °C, protected from light).
Incubate the mixture at RT on the roller for 1 h; the solution should remain brownish.
Use the solution immediately on tubuloids or store up to 24 h at 4 °C protected from light.

steps.title: Produce Conditioned Media
steps.instruction: Generate Wnt3a‑ and R‑spondin‑1‑conditioned media from engineered cell lines for tubuloid culture.

substeps.instruction: Thaw Wnt3a‑producing L cells and R‑spondin‑1‑producing HEK‑293T cells; seed each in a 10 cm dish with DMEM high glucose + 10 % FBS.
After 24 h, replace the medium with zeocin selection medium.
Culture under zeocin selection for ≥7 days, splitting when confluence reaches ~80 %.
Post‑selection, split each line into a 15 cm dish containing DMEM high glucose + 10 % FBS.
When cells reach ~80 % confluence, replace medium with conditioning medium (same base as tubuloid culture medium) and culture for ≥7 days without passaging.
Collect the conditioned media, centrifuge at 400 g for 5 min at RT, and transfer the supernatant.
Filter the supernatant through a sterile 0.22 µm Filtropur BT 50 filter.
Optional: Verify biological activity via TOP‑FLASH assay (mix 30 % Wnt3a‑CM, 10 % R‑spondin‑1‑CM, 60 % DMEM; activity should be >30‑fold over control).
Aliquot and store at –80 °C for up to 1 year; after thawing keep at 4 °C for no longer than 2 weeks.

steps.title: Prepare Tubuloid Culture Medium
steps.instruction: Make tubuloid culture medium under sterile conditions and use within one week of preparation.

steps.title: Prepare Kidney Digestion Buffer
steps.instruction: Create fresh digestion buffer for mouse kidney dissociation (10 ml per kidney pair).

substeps.instruction: Weigh collagenase and add DMEM to a final collagenase concentration of 1 mg ml⁻¹ in a 50 ml tube.
Add deoxyribonuclease to reach 60 U ml⁻¹.
Add liberase to reach 0.2 mg ml⁻¹.
Use 10 ml of this buffer for each pair of kidneys; prepare the buffer on the day of use.

steps.title: Prepare Propidium Iodide Solution
steps.instruction: Make a 25 µg ml⁻¹ PI staining solution for tubuloid injury assessment.

substeps.instruction: Reconstitute PI powder in DMSO to 10 mg ml⁻¹.
Dilute 1:20 with PBS to obtain 500 µg ml⁻¹ stock.
On staining day, thaw the 500 µg ml⁻¹ stock and dilute 1:20 with tubuloid culture medium to reach 25 µg ml⁻¹.
Store PI solutions at –20 °C protected from light.

steps.title: Stain Tubuloids and Quantify Injury
steps.instruction: Assess myoglobin‑induced tubuloid damage by PI staining and image analysis.

substeps.instruction: Remove culture medium from the 8‑well μ‑Slide (IBIDI) and wash wells twice with PBS (RT, 5 min each) on a circular vibrating shaker.
Add 200 µl of the 25 µg ml⁻¹ PI solution to each well and incubate 30 min on the shaker, protected from light.
Acquire bright‑field and fluorescence images using a microscope equipped with a camera (e.g., Leica Thunder).
Count the total number of PI foci per tubuloid to quantify tubular damage.

description: Organoids are self-organizing three-dimensional structures grown from stem or progenitor cells that recapitulate key features of the tissues they originate from. Importantly, organoids have also become a widely-applied tool to model diseases. For example, primary renal tubular epithelial organoids, termed “tubuloids”, grown from adult kidney tissue have been used to study BK virus infection; moreover, renal “tumoroids” have been derived from Wilms tumors (=nephroblastoma), the most common pediatric solid cancer.2 Very recently, renal tubuloids have been employed to model acute kidney injury (AKI), a frequent clinical condition associated with high morbidity and mortality.3 AKI can be triggered by various pathological conditions, including rhabdomyolysis, i.e., muscle cell necrosis resulting in release of the muscle protein, myoglobin, which causes acute tubular injury. Tubuloids can be harnessed to identify functionally relevant molecular mechanisms through which renal tubular epithelial cells (mal-)adapt to myoglobin-induced stress.1 Moreover, they can be used to assess the effect of pharmacological drugs on myoglobin-induced injury. Here, we describe the experimental steps to establish and propagate renal tubuloid cultures from the mouse renal cortex, and to induce and quantify myoglobinuric injury.
